item.title: WordPress wp2shell CVEs get exploits as Microsoft warns of ACR Stealer surge
On-Device Age Verification and Squarespace Unicode Phishing Bypass
WordPress wp2shell Exploits, 7-Zip RCE Patch, ACR Stealer Surge, DPRK Developer Lures
item.content:encoded:
WordPress Core "wp2shell" RCE flaws get public exploits, patch now — Must Read

Public exploits are now available for the critical WordPress Core “wp2shell” flaws that can enable unauthenticated remote code execution on affected 6.9.x and 7.0.x sites. Administrators should immediately update to WordPress 7.0.2 or 6.9.5, with WAF or REST API blocking only as temporary mitigation.

  • Public proof-of-concept exploits have been released for the critical “wp2shell” remote code execution vulnerabilities affecting WordPress Core.
  • The wp2shell attack chains CVE-2026-63030, a REST API batch-route confusion flaw, with CVE-2026-60137, an SQL injection flaw in the author__not_in parameter of WP_Query.
  • The complete remote code execution chain affects WordPress 6.9.0 through 6.9.4 and WordPress 7.0.0 through 7.0.1, and it has been fixed in WordPress 6.9.5 and 7.0.2.
  • WordPress has enabled forced automatic security updates for supported installations running affected versions and urged site owners to update immediately.
  • Cloudflare deployed WAF protections for both vulnerabilities, while watchTowr said it has seen public exploit code in circulation and the first signs of in-the-wild exploitation.

New North Korean campaign uses fake coding interviews to steal developer credentials — Must Read

Elastic Security Labs uncovered a DPRK-aligned Contagious Interview campaign that lures developers with fake coding challenges and hides OTTERCOOKIE-like malware inside SVG files. Running the trojanized projects can steal browser credentials, crypto wallets, sensitive files and clipboard data while installing a Socket.IO-based remote access backdoor.

  • Elastic Security Labs discovered a new DPRK-aligned Contagious Interview campaign, tracked as REF9403, after a fake recruiter posted a job offer in its community Slack workspace and sent developers a trojanized coding challenge.
  • The trojanized projects hid Base64-encoded payload fragments inside HTML comments across SVG flag images, then reassembled and executed the payload when the project server started.
  • Running the malicious project delivered four OTTERCOOKIE-aligned capabilities: a browser credential and crypto wallet stealer, a file stealer, a Socket.IO-based remote access trojan, and a clipboard stealer.
  • The malware targeted developer machines across Windows, macOS, and Linux by collecting browser data, wallet extension databases, sensitive files, shell histories, cloud and SSH configuration paths, and macOS keychain data.
  • Elastic linked the activity to Contagious Interview based on code similarity, behavior, and infrastructure overlapping with prior reporting on OTTERCOOKIE and related DPRK campaigns.

Microsoft warns of surge in ACR Stealer attacks on customers — Must Read

Microsoft says ACR Stealer attacks are surging against enterprise customers, using ClickFix lures, WebDAV, MSHTA, and obfuscated PowerShell to steal browser credentials, tokens, and business documents. Organizations should restrict risky script/tool execution and web-based delivery paths to reduce exposure.

  • Microsoft observed a surge between late April and mid-June in attacks using ACR Stealer to steal browser-stored passwords, authentication tokens, and sensitive documents from enterprise customers.
  • The threat actor used ClickFix social engineering, WebDAV servers, and the MSHTA utility to deliver the ACR Stealer payload.
  • One common intrusion chain uses a ClickFix lure to run a malicious DLL from a remote WebDAV share with rundll32.exe, followed by obfuscated PowerShell, a bundled Python loader, persistence through a scheduled task, and in-memory payload execution.
  • A second common intrusion chain uses ClickFix to launch MSHTA, retrieve malicious content from the attacker’s server, run an obfuscated PowerShell downloader, and execute an encrypted payload hidden inside a publicly hosted JPEG image.
  • Microsoft recommends defenses including avoiding copied command instructions from websites, filtering or blocking low-reputation and new domains, restricting unnecessary online resources, and using application control rules for tools such as PowerShell, Python, mshta.exe, and rundll32.exe.

Update now: 7-Zip fixes RCE flaw exploitable with malicious archives — Must Read

7-Zip 26.02 fixes a remote code execution flaw in its XZ decompression handling that could be triggered by a malicious archive. Because 7-Zip does not auto-update, users should manually install the latest version from the official site.

  • 7-Zip version 26.02 was released to fix a remote code execution vulnerability in the program’s processing of XZ-compressed data.
  • The Zero Day Initiative advisory says specially crafted XZ data can trigger a heap-based buffer overflow that may allow attackers to execute arbitrary code as the user.
  • Exploitation requires user interaction, such as visiting a malicious page or opening a malicious archive file.
  • 7-Zip does not include an automatic update feature, so users must manually download and install the latest version from 7-zip.org.
  • There are currently no reports that attackers are actively exploiting this newly disclosed 7-Zip vulnerability.

The Squarespace Phish With No Brand Text to Match — Should Read

A Squarespace phishing email bypassed brand-text detection by hiding the brand name with invisible Unicode characters and placing it only inside an image, while passing SPF, DKIM, and DMARC through a hijacked aged domain. It was ultimately caught through behavioral signals such as malicious link reputation, sender anomalies, and OCR/image-based detection.

  • A credential-harvesting email impersonating Squarespace reached a K-12 school district and used a fake billing notice to warn that a domain would be deactivated in two days.
  • The word “Squarespace” did not appear as machine-readable text in the message because the logo and wordmark were delivered as an image and the subject and sender display name were padded with invisible U+206E characters.
  • The message passed SPF, DKIM, and DMARC because it was sent from the hijacked 24-year-old domain oldanopetroli[.]com through Aliyun DirectMail infrastructure.
  • The payment link led to a tokenized subdomain on compromised studiointech[.]net, which was flagged malicious.
  • IRONSCALES Themis flagged the incident at 90% confidence as Credential Theft and Image-Based Attack and automatically resolved it as phishing before anyone in the district acted on it.

The Future of Age Verification: Your Face Never Leaves Your Device — Optional

Incode is promoting an on-device age verification system that estimates age and checks liveness locally so users’ face images are not transmitted or stored. The company positions this as a privacy-preserving way for platforms to meet expanding age assurance laws while still detecting spoofing and tampering.

  • Incode says more than 30 age assurance laws are now in force worldwide, including requirements in the UK, Australia, Brazil, and about half of U.S. states.
  • Incode’s On-Device Age Estimation runs facial age estimation and passive liveness detection on a user’s phone, tablet, or laptop so the face is not transmitted or stored.
  • The system sends only the outcome of whether the user meets the platform’s required age threshold, while server-side checks analyze session metadata for tampering and injection attempts without facial or biometric data.
  • Incode announced a $100 million commitment to privacy-preserving identity infrastructure alongside its acquisition of Identiq, which developed technology for sharing fraud signals without exposing customer data to a third party.
  • The article states that Incode’s models have processed more than 7 billion trust checks and that its security layer achieves 99% spoof detection across deepfakes, injection attacks, replay attacks, and physical spoofing.
